English

WOTD – 19 September 2026

Etymology

Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *úp
Proto-Indo-European *-er
Proto-Indo-European *upér
Proto-Italic *super
Latin super
Latin super-lbor.
English super-
Proto-Indo-European *nu
Proto-Indo-European *néwos
Proto-Italic *nowos
Latin novusder.
English nova
English supernova

    From super- (prefix meaning ‘exceptionally large in quantity, excessive; superior in potency or power’) + nova (“sudden brightening of a previously inconspicuous star”),[1] coined by the German astronomer Walter Baade (1893–1960) and the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky (1898–1974) who introduced the term in an astrophysics course and in seminars at the California Institute of Technology in 1931,[2] although it was the Swedish astronomer Knut Lundmark (1889–1958) who first used the word in print in a paper dated 31 December 1932 and published in 1933:[3] see the quotation.

      • (Received Pronunciation) IPA(key): /ˈsuːpəˌnəʊvə/, /ˌsuːpəˈnəʊvə/

      • (General American) IPA(key): /ˌsupəɹˈnəʊvi/, /ˈsupəɹˌnəʊvi/
      • Hyphenation: sup‧er‧no‧vae

    Noun

    supernova (plural supernovae or (archaic) supernovæ or supernovas)

    1. (astronomy) A bright and powerful explosion of a massive star which is sudden but brief, and causes the ejection of most or all of the star's matter and the emission of radiation; afterwards, the star becomes a black hole or a neutron star, or is destroyed. [from 1930s]
      Synonym: (abbreviation) SN
      Hyponyms: fast-evolving luminous transient, kilonova, macronova, stripped-envelope supernova
      • 1932 December 31 (date written), Knut Lundmark, “The Pre-Tychonic Novae”, in Lund Observatory Circular, number 8, Lund, Scania, Sweden: Lund Observatory, published January 1933, →OCLC, page 218:
        But taking mmax‾=1 we find: / Mmax=−13.5, / which places the objects among the "upper class" or super-Novae.
        According to the Oxford English Dictionary, this is the earliest attestation of the word in print.
      • 1934 May 15, W[alter] Baade, F[ritz] Zwicky, “On Super-novae”, in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, volume 20, number 5, Washington, D.C.: National Academy of Sciences, →DOI, →ISSN, →OCLC, pages 254–255:
        [page 254] The extensive investigations of extragalactic systems during recent years have brought to light the remarkable fact that there exist two well-defined types of new stars or novae which might be distinguished as common novae and super-novae. […] [page 255] Regarding the initial states of super-novae only the following meager facts are known. First, super-novae occur not only in the blurred central parts of nebulae but also in the spiral arms, which in certain cases are clearly resolved into individual stars. Secondly, the super-nova of 1572 in its initial stage probably was not brighter than apparent magnitude 5 as otherwise it would be registered as such in the old catalogues, which, however, is not the case. Super-novae are a much less frequent phenomenon than common novae. So far as the present observational evidence goes, their frequency is of the order of one super-nova per stellar system (nebula) per several centuries.
      • 1983–1984 (date recorded), Peter Gill, Holly Johnson, Mark O’Toole, Brian Nash, “Welcome To The Pleasuredome”, in Welcome to the Pleasuredome, performed by Frankie Goes to Hollywood, London: ZTT Records, published 29 October 1984, →OCLC:
        Shooting stars never stop even when they reach the top / There goes a supernova / What a pushover, yeah
      • 1985, Isaac Asimov, “Bigger Explosions”, in The Exploding Suns: The Secrets of the Supernovas (Truman Talley Books), New York, N.Y.: E[dward] P[ayson] Dutton, →ISBN, page 97:
        Supernovas are clearly incredible objects of astoundingly explosive character. Were it possible for our Sun to go supernova, it would vaporize every planet in the solar system by the time it had reached peak brilliance. Were it possible for Alpha Centauri, which is only 1.3 parsecs away, to go supernova, it would blaze in our day and night sky with a brightness that, at maximum, would be 15,500 times that of the full Moon, or about one-thirtieth that of the Sun.
      • 1991, Douglas Coupland, “Plastics Never Disintegrate”, in Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture, New York, N.Y.: St. Martin’s Press, →ISBN, page 162:
        Dumpster clocking: The tendency when looking at objects to guesstimate the amount of time they will take to decompose: "Ski boots are the worst. Solid plastic. They'll be around till the sun goes supernova."
      • 1995 February–June (date recorded), Noel Gallagher, “Champagne Supernova”, in (What’s the Story) Morning Glory?, performed by Oasis, London: Creation Records, published 2 October 1995, →OCLC:
        Someday you will find me / Caught beneath the landslide / In a champagne supernova / A champagne supernova in the sky
      • 2024 August 21, Ashley Strickland, “An Unusual Object is Moving so Fast It could Escape the Milky Way. Scientists aren’t Certain what It is”, in CNN‎, archived from the original on 1 March 2026:
        In these stellar pairings, if the two stars are close together, the white dwarf will siphon mass away from its companion and have an outburst called a nova. And when the white dwarf accumulates too much mass, it will collapse and explode in a supernova. "In this kind of supernova, the white dwarf is completely destroyed, so its companion is released and flies off at whatever orbital speed it was originally moving, plus a little bit of a kick from the supernova explosion as well," [Adam] Burgasser said.
    2. (figurative) Something which is brilliant or explosive.
      • 1962 July 19, Geminus [pseudonym], “It Seems to Me”, in New Scientist, volume 15, number 296, London: Harrison, Raison and Co., →ISSN, →OCLC, page 155, column 1:
        For my taste Mr [Peter] Thorneycroft is a less heartening supernova. […] Unfortunately, however, I am jaundiced. In his zealous devotion to European causes Mr Thorneycroft has frequently used schemes for technical development as a means to a political end.
      • 2024 February 22, Jake Henry Smith, “Butter Yellow will be Everywhere this Year—Here’s How to Style It”, in Glamour‎, New York, N.Y.: Condé Nast, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 15 May 2026:
        Butter yellow (yes, the pastel between canary and beige) has been on the rise for the past few years, and we've seen it splashed across enough recent runways and style influencers to finally make a call: The soft, silky shade is about to go supernova.

      Norwegian Bokmål

      Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
      supernova
      Wikipedia no

      Etymology

      Internationalism; see English supernova. The complete term is attested in English astronomical writing by 1933.[1] By surface analysis, super- (“exceptionally powerful”) +‎ nova (“nova”).

      The first element ultimately derives from Latin super- (“above, beyond”), from super, itself from Proto-Italic *super, from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“over, above”). The second derives from Latin nova, the feminine of novus (“new”), in stella nova (“new star”); novus continues Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”).[2]

      Compare the corresponding international terms Norwegian Nynorsk supernova, Danish supernova, German Supernova, French supernova and English supernova.

      Pronunciation

      • IPA(key): /¹sʉː.pərˌnoː.ʋa/, [ˈsʉ̀ː.pəˌɳoː.ʋa][3]
      • Rhymes: -oːʋa
      • Hyphenation: su‧per‧no‧va

      Noun

      supernova m (definite singular supernovaen, indefinite plural supernovaer, definite plural supernovaene)

      1. (astronomy) supernova; an extremely powerful stellar explosion, or a star undergoing such an explosion.
        Astronomene oppdaget en supernova i en fjern galakse. ― The astronomers discovered a supernova in a distant galaxy.
        • 2000, Vigdis Hjorth, Hva er det med mor, page 19:
          hun lengter bort, sier hun, ut av solsystemet, mot […] eksploderende supernovaer, andre galakser
          she longs to get away, she says, out of the solar system, towards […] exploding supernovae, other galaxies
        • 2021, Petter Callin et al., ERGO Fysikk 1, page 465:
          restene etter en supernova kan vi se som en lysende gassky […]
          we can see the remains of a supernova as a glowing cloud of gas […]
